title: Lemon balm
subtitle: The gentle nervine: infusions, tinctures, and glycerites for anxiety and nervous digestion
excerpt: Lemon balm is the lemon-scented mint-family herb whose fresh and dried leaves make the most approachable nervine in the home garden. The leaves are brewed as a calming infusion, extracted as a tincture, or prepared as an alcohol-free glycerite for children and adults who avoid alcohol. Dried lemon balm keeps 12 months in a sealed tin; the fresh herb is available from the garden from late spring through autumn.

glossaryTerms.definition: A herb traditionally used to support the nervous system, calming tension, easing anxiety, or improving sleep. Lemon balm is one of the gentlest nervines in the European home tradition.
An alcohol-free herbal extract made by macerating herb in food-grade vegetable glycerine and water. Suited to those who avoid alcohol; sweet-tasting and suitable for children.

content.text: Melissa officinalis L., family Lamiaceae. A leafy perennial herb, 30 to 80 cm, with soft, deeply veined, pale green leaves that smell unmistakably of lemon when crushed. Small white or cream flowers appear in clusters at the leaf axils in summer. Native to the eastern Mediterranean and central Asia. naturalised throughout temperate Europe and the Americas. Grows readily in a pot or garden border. may spread aggressively in warm conditions. The fresh or dried leaf is the part used, avoid stems and woody parts.

The leaf carries a volatile oil (the source of the lemon scent), rosmarinic acid, caffeic acid, flavonoids, and tannins. Current herbal guidance focuses on the volatile oil and rosmarinic acid for the calming and muscle-easing actions. Rosmarinic acid may inhibit an enzyme that breaks down GABA (a calming chemical in the brain). The action on smooth muscle supports the traditional use for nervous digestive symptoms.

The 17th-century herbalist Culpeper described lemon balm for nervous conditions and low spirits. The 20th-century herbalist Grieve records its use in balm tea for nervousness, low spirits, and headaches. John Evelyn called it sovereign for the brain. The Eclectic tradition used melissa for nervous tension and low mood. Current herbal guidance supports traditional use for mild anxiety, stress, poor sleep, and nervous digestive complaints.

Hot infusion: 1 to 2 teaspoons of dried leaf (or a generous handful of fresh leaf) per 200 ml of just-boiled water, steeped covered for 8 to 10 minutes. The lid keeps the aromatic oils from escaping. Drink one to three cups a day, or one cup taken 30 to 60 minutes before bed for sleep.
Herbal extract: 1 part fresh leaf to 2 parts 40% spirit, or 1 part dried leaf to 5 parts 40% spirit. steep 4 to 6 weeks, strain. Dose: 3 to 5 ml in a little water, up to three times daily.

Glycerite (alcohol-free): 1 part fresh or dried leaf to 2 parts vegetable glycerine. Warm gently and steep for 2 to 4 weeks. Strain through muslin. Dose: 3 to 5 ml in a little water. Sweet-tasting and right for children under herbalist guidance and for those who avoid alcohol.

Thyroid conditions: lemon balm may affect thyroid function. If you have a thyroid condition or take thyroid medicine, ask your doctor before using it as a daily drink. Occasional tea is unlikely to matter.

General tolerance: lemon balm is one of the best-tolerated herbs in the western home tradition. At the doses and preparations above, it is right for adults and older children (8 and above, under herbalist guidance). The main risk is in those with thyroid conditions taking the herb without awareness of the interaction.
